steps.cap:
Six plasma levels are plotted against time and joined by straight lines.
There is no equation for this curve, only the measured points, so the area is estimated from the points.

The question asks for the AUC from 2 to 4 hours, so only the rows at 2, 3 and 4 hours are used.
The 0.5 and 1 hour rows are before the interval and the 5 hour row is after it; none of them enters the sum.

Each strip is a trapezoid: its area is the average of its two heights times its width.
From 2 to 3 hr: {{frac:18.4 + 11.1|2}} × 1 hr = 14.75 mcg·hr/mL.

From 3 to 4 hr: {{frac:11.1 + 6.77|2}} × 1 hr = 8.935 mcg·hr/mL.
The width is read from the time column each time; here both strips are 1 hour wide.

AUC from 2 to 4 hr = 14.75 + 8.935 = 23.685, reported as 23.7 mcg·hr/mL.
The unit is concentration times time: mcg/mL × hr = mcg·hr/mL.

auc_steps.title: The trapezoidal rule on her data, one strip at a time

steps.cap:
A 50 mg dose was given by IV bolus, all at once into a vein. The six measured concentrations, 2.52, 1.59, 1.00, 0.64, 0.40 and 0.25 mg/L at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5 and 3 hr, are plotted on a log axis.
They fall on a straight line, so the drug is eliminated by a first-order process (a fixed fraction leaves each hour). One compartment, the whole body treated as one evenly mixed space, describes it.

k, the elimination rate constant, is the slope of the log line. Between 1 and 2 hr: k = {{frac:ln 1.59 − ln 0.64|2 hr − 1 hr}} = 0.91 hr⁻¹.
The half-life, the time for the concentration to halve: t½ = {{frac:0.693|0.91 hr⁻¹}} = 0.76 hr.

C0 is the concentration the dose would give at time zero, before any elimination. It is read by extending the line back to t = 0.
From her 2.5-hr point: C0 = 0.40 × e^(0.91 × 2.5) = 3.89 mg/L.

VD, the apparent volume of distribution, is the dose over C0: VD = {{frac:50 mg|3.89 mg/L}} = 12.85 L.
ClT, total body clearance, is the volume cleared of drug per hour: ClT = k × VD = 0.91 × 12.85 = 11.7 L/hr.

The amount in the body at 3 hr is the volume times the concentration: 12.85 L × 0.25 mg/L = 3.2 mg.
Each half-life removes half of what is left, so ten half-lives leave 0.1%: 99.9% is gone at 10 × 0.76 = 7.6 hr.

bolus1_steps.title: One-compartment IV bolus, from her data to every answer

steps.cap:
Drug runs in at a constant rate, R = 44.35 mg/hr, chosen so the plateau will be 20 mg/L. A constant rate in is a zero-order input.
Elimination is first order: a fixed fraction leaves each hour. The elimination rate constant is k = {{frac:0.693|t½}} = {{frac:0.693|5 hr}} = 0.1386 hr⁻¹, t½ being the half-life, the time for the level to fall by half. So the amount leaving per hour grows as the level grows.
VD, the apparent volume of distribution, is 16 L. Three hours in: C = {{frac:R|VD × k}}(1 − e^(−kt)) = {{frac:44.35|16 × 0.1386}}(1 − e^(−0.1386 × 3)) = 6.8 mg/L, her part 3.

Css, the steady-state concentration, is where rate in equals rate out: Css = {{frac:R|k × VD}} = {{frac:44.35|0.1386 × 16}} = 20 mg/L.
The climb is set by the half-life alone. After 1 half-life (5 hr) the level is half of Css, 10.0; after 3 half-lives (15 hr) 87.5%, 17.5; after 5 half-lives (25 hr) 96.9%, 19.4.
A faster rate would raise the plateau, not shorten the climb.

Her part 4: the infusion is switched off at 3 hr, at 6.8 mg/L. Nothing comes in, so the level falls by first-order elimination alone.
Four hours later: C = 6.8 × e^(−0.1386 × 4) = 3.9 mg/L.

infusion_steps.title: IV infusion: the climb to steady state, and the fall when it stops

loading_steps.footer: In-Class IV Infusions - Solutions.pdf, parts 1 and 2

steps.cap:
DL, the loading dose, is the amount in the body at steady state, the plateau the infusion is set to hold. Css is the target steady-state concentration, 20 mg/L, and VD the apparent volume of distribution, 16 L. DL = Css × VD = 20 mg/L × 16 L = 320 mg, her part 1.
On its own that bolus starts at {{frac:320 mg|16 L}} = 20 mg/L and falls by first-order elimination (a fixed fraction lost per hour). The elimination rate constant is k = {{frac:0.693|5 hr}} = 0.1386 hr⁻¹, the half-life being 5 hr: at 3 hr, 20 × e^(−0.1386 × 3) = 13.2 mg/L.
The infusion on its own, at the rate R = 44.35 mg/hr, climbs toward Css as {{frac:R|VD × k}}(1 − e^(−kt)). At 3 hr: {{frac:44.35|16 × 0.1386}}(1 − e^(−0.1386 × 3)) = 6.8 mg/L.

The two run at once, so the concentrations add: 13.2 + 6.8 = 20 mg/L at 3 hr, her part 2.
What the bolus part loses each hour the infusion part gains, so the sum stays at Css from the first minute.

The infusion alone reaches 90% of Css only when 1 − e^(−kt) = 0.9, at t = {{frac:ln 10|0.1386 hr⁻¹}} = 16.6 hr.
The loading dose replaces that wait; it does not change the plateau, which the rate sets.

loading_steps.title: Loading dose with an infusion: why the level is flat from the start

steps.cap:
Dose 1, 10 mg/kg, arrives at time zero; the same dose follows every 8 hours. C0, the concentration one dose produces on its own, is the dose over the apparent volume of distribution, VD 0.25 L/kg: C0 = {{frac:10 mg/kg|0.25 L/kg}} = 40 mg/L.
The half-life, the time for the concentration to fall by half, is 4 hr, so eight hours is two half-lives.
So 40 mg/L halves to 20, then to 10 mg/L just before dose 2.

Dose 2 adds another 40 mg/L to the 10 mg/L still present: 10 + 40 = 50.0 mg/L.
Over the next 8 hours that 50.0 falls by two half-lives to 12.5 mg/L by 16 hr.

Each dose adds 40 mg/L to a larger remainder, so each peak is higher than the last by a smaller amount.
The peaks climb 40.0, 50.0, 52.5, 53.1, 53.3, 53.3 mg/L and stop climbing.

The climb is over within 3 to 5 half-lives, here 12 to 20 hours. This is steady state: each dose now replaces exactly what was lost.
At steady state the curve repeats between the peak, Cmax 53.3 mg/L, and the trough, Cmin 13.3 mg/L: 53.3 halved twice over the two half-lives of the interval.
The average over an interval is Cavg = {{frac:dose|VD × k × τ}} = {{frac:10 mg/kg|0.25 L/kg × 0.173 hr⁻¹ × 8 hr}} = 28.9 mg/L. k, the elimination rate constant, is {{frac:0.693|4 hr}} = 0.173 hr⁻¹; τ, the dosing interval, is 8 hr. Cavg sits below the midpoint of 33.3 mg/L, {{frac:53.3 + 13.3|2}}, because the curve spends more of each interval at the lower concentrations.

After the sixth dose no more drug comes in.
The level falls by first-order elimination alone, halving every 4 hours.

md_bolus_steps.title: Repeated IV bolus, dose by dose

steps.cap:
Each dose is 250 mg by mouth; F = 0.75 of it reaches the blood. VD, the apparent volume of distribution, is 1.5 L/kg × 75 kg = 112.5 L.
The elimination half-life, the time for the level to fall by half, is 10 hr, so the elimination rate constant k = {{frac:0.693|10 hr}} = 0.0693 hr⁻¹. The absorption rate constant, the fraction of the unabsorbed dose entering the blood per hour, is ka = 0.9 hr⁻¹. So each dose on its own rises to a peak and falls, like a single oral dose.
First-dose tmax, the time of the peak, = {{frac:ln(ka ÷ k)|ka − k}} = {{frac:ln(0.9 ÷ 0.0693)|0.9 − 0.0693}} = 3.1 hr. Cmax, the peak concentration, = {{frac:F ka D0|VD (ka − k)}}(e^(−k tmax) − e^(−ka tmax)) = 1.35 mg/L, her answers (D0 is the 250 mg dose).

Dose 2 at 8 hr adds its own curve on top of what is left of dose 1 (superposition: later doses do not change k, ka, F or VD).
So the second peak is higher than the first, and the level just before dose 3 is higher than it was before dose 2.

Every dose adds the same curve to a larger remainder. The half-life is 10 hr, so the climb is over within 3 to 5 half-lives, 30 to 50 hours.
τ is the dosing interval, 8 hr. The accumulation factor {{frac:1|1 − e^(−kτ)}} = {{frac:1|1 − e^(−0.0693 × 8)}} = 2.35 says how much higher the steady-state peak sits than the first-dose peak.

At steady state (∞ marks it) the peak comes earlier in the interval. tmax∞ = {{frac:1|ka − k}} ln[{{frac:ka(1 − e^(−kτ))|k(1 − e^(−ka τ))}}] = 2.06 hr after a dose, her answer, against 3.1 hr for the first dose.
Cmax∞ = {{frac:F D0|VD}}({{frac:1|1 − e^(−kτ)}})e^(−k tmax∞) = 3.40 mg/L. Cmin∞, at the end of the interval, = {{frac:ka F D0|VD (ka − k)}}({{frac:1|1 − e^(−kτ)}})e^(−kτ) = 2.44 mg/L. Cavg∞ = {{frac:F D0|VD k τ}} = 3.01 mg/L.
Her spoken values were about 3.3, 2.4 and 3; these are what her inputs give.

md_oral_steps.title: Multiple oral doses, dose by dose: her tetracycline example

steps.cap:
Only F = 0.85 of the 500 mg tablet reaches the blood. It enters by first-order absorption: a fixed fraction of what is still in the gut enters each hour. The absorption rate constant ka is 0.693 over the absorption half-life of 0.75 hr (45 min): ka = {{frac:0.693|0.75 hr}} = 0.924 hr⁻¹.
It leaves by first-order elimination (a fixed fraction of what is in the body leaves each hour). The elimination rate constant k is 0.693 over the elimination half-life of 3 hr: k = {{frac:0.693|3 hr}} = 0.231 hr⁻¹. Early on far more enters per hour than leaves, so the level rises.

tmax, the time of the peak, depends on the two rate constants only: tmax = {{frac:ln(ka ÷ k)|ka − k}} = {{frac:ln 4|0.693}} = 2.0 hr.
Cmax, the peak concentration, is the curve at tmax, with D0 the 500 mg dose and VD, the apparent volume of distribution, 22 L. Cmax = {{frac:F ka D0|VD (ka − k)}}(e^(−k tmax) − e^(−ka tmax)). With the numbers in: {{frac:0.85 × 0.924 × 500|22 × 0.693}}(e^(−0.231 × 2) − e^(−0.924 × 2)) = 12.17 mg/L, her answer.
At the peak the rate of absorption equals the rate of elimination.

After tmax more leaves per hour than enters, so the level falls. At 8 hr: 4.04 mg/L.
Once the absorption site is empty the fall is elimination alone, with the slope k.

The equation is a difference of two exponentials with the same front factor, {{frac:F ka D0|VD (ka − k)}} = 25.76 mg/L.
The elimination term, 25.76 e^(−kt), falls slowly; the absorption term, 25.76 e^(−ka t), falls fast. The curve is the first minus the second.
The front factor is not C0 (the time-zero concentration an IV bolus of the same amount would give): no concentration on an oral curve is ever as high as it.
steps.tag: the two terms behind the curve

oral_steps.title: A single oral dose, from her Example 1 to the peak and beyond

steps.cap:
From 0 to 2 hr the first infusion runs. Its rate R is the dose over the infusion time: R = {{frac:300 mg|2 hr}} = 150 mg/hr.
While it runs, the level climbs as a single infusion does: C = {{frac:R|VD × k}}(1 − e^(−kt)). VD is the apparent volume of distribution, 15 L; k is the elimination rate constant, the fraction lost per hour, 0.15 hr⁻¹.
With t = 2 hr, the end of the infusion, that gives {{frac:150|15 × 0.15}}(1 − e^(−0.3)) = 17.28 mg/L.

With the infusion off, nothing comes in and the level falls by first-order elimination (a fixed fraction lost per hour) from 17.28 mg/L.
At 6 hr, four hours after it stopped: 17.28 × e^(−0.15 × 4) = 17.28 × e^(−0.6) = 9.48 mg/L.

The second infusion starts at 6 hr and builds exactly as the first did, to 17.28 mg/L at 8 hr.
By 8 hr, six hours after it stopped, the leftover of dose 1 has fallen to 17.28 × e^(−0.15 × 6) = 7.03 mg/L.
The plasma level at 8 hr is the sum of the two: 17.28 + 7.03 = 24.30 mg/L.

At 12 hr dose 1 has been declining for 10 hr since it stopped and gives 3.86 mg/L.
Dose 2 has been declining for 4 hr since it stopped and gives 9.48 mg/L.
The plasma concentration is the sum: 3.86 + 9.48 = 13.34 mg/L.

two_infusions_steps.title: Two intermittent IV infusions, stage by stage

steps.cap:
After the bolus the drug is all in the central compartment (the blood and the organs it reaches at once). It then moves into a tissue compartment and back, and leaves from the central one.
On a log axis the curve is steep at first, while drug is still spreading into tissue, then becomes one straight line once the two compartments are in balance.
The curve is Cp = 12e^(−5.8t) + 18e^(−0.16t), two exponential terms. C0, the concentration at time zero, is the sum of their two intercepts, the numbers in front: 12 + 18 = 30 mg/L.

The straight part is the elimination phase, 18 e^(−0.16t). Extending it back to t = 0 gives the intercept B = 18 mg/L; its slope is β = 0.16 hr⁻¹.
β sets the elimination half-life: t½β = {{frac:0.693|0.16 hr⁻¹}} = 4.33 hr.

Subtracting the terminal line from the early part of the curve leaves the distribution term, 12 e^(−5.8t): intercept A = 12 mg/L, slope α = 5.8 hr⁻¹.
α is the larger constant, so this term is gone within an hour; that is why the early fall is steep.

Put t = 3 into both terms: 12 × e^(−5.8 × 3) = 0.0000, effectively nothing, and 18 × e^(−0.16 × 3) = 11.14.
Cp at 3 hr = 11.14 mg/L, her answer. Only the β term is left by then.
